intro: Lesson 25: Erosional landforms: headlands, bays, cliffs and stacks (2.1c). Read the ideas from the lesson, then do the tasks.

panels.title: Headlands and bays
points: Discordant coast: hard and soft rock bands

model.title: Explain the formation of a stack. (4 marks)

parts.text: Hydraulic action and abrasion widen a joint in a headland into a cave (1)
Caves on both sides join to form an arch (1)
Weathering and erosion weaken the arch roof until it collapses (1)
An isolated pillar of rock remains: a stack (1)

parts.label: Why it works
parts.text: Four linked points with process terms

keywords.def: a section of hard rock sticking out to sea
a curved inlet of softer rock between headlands
rock bands at right angles to the coast
a flat rocky area left as a cliff retreats
a pillar of rock left when an arch collapses

questions.q: Describe the features of a wave-cut platform. (2 marks)
questions.a: Flat, gently sloping rocky area at the cliff foot (1), exposed at low tide, with rock pools (1)

questions.q: Core: Annotated sequence diagram of cave, arch, stack, stump, then answer: 'Explain the formation of headlands and bays.' (4 marks)
questions.a: Discordant geology; differential erosion; soft rock forms bays, hard rock left as headlands; processes named

questions.q: Extend: Use an OS map extract of the Dorset coast to give six-figure grid references of a stack and a bay.
Stretch: Why does Durdle Door's arch survive while others collapse? (3 marks)
questions.a: Rock strength, joints and wave energy vary; collapse depends on weaknesses
B) Soft rock. Softer rock erodes faster than the headlands either side.

questions.q: Old Harry Rocks is an example of a:
Big question: will Old Harry Rocks stand in 500 years?
questions.a: Not unchanged: erosion and weathering will keep wearing it, turning stacks to stumps over time
